conceited

kuhn-SEE-tid · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Conceited is excessively proud of oneself in general — of one's talents, importance, and looks alike.

Nobody wanted to be paired with the conceited debate captain, who spent every practice reminding the team of his own undefeated record.

Worked Example

The conceited actor insisted his dressing room mirror be replaced with a larger one, certain the old frame didn't do his reflection justice.

Conceited describes an excessive, often obvious pride in one's own looks or abilities -- more than simple confidence.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

vain: Vain means having excessive pride in one specific thing -- almost always your appearance, sometimes a single prized talent. Conceited is wider: a conceited person is excessively proud of themselves in general, looks and talents and importance all at once. Vanity fixates on one department; conceit covers the whole person.

arrogant: Arrogant means having an exaggerated sense of your own importance and treating other people as beneath you -- arrogance always looks down on somebody. Conceited pride can be self-contained: a conceited person may simply advertise and admire themselves without dismissing anyone. Arrogance needs a target; conceit only needs an audience.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

humble: having a modest view of one's own importance

modest: not boastful about one's abilities

Where it sits · how swollen the ego gets — confident → conceited → narcissistic

confident vs. conceited: Confident simply means self-assured, without the excessive, often obnoxious pride that conceited implies.

narcissistic vs. conceited: Narcissistic goes further than conceited, describing an all-consuming self-obsession that ignores other people's feelings entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: with, together (intensifying) (Latin)

Root — ceit

Root — ceit: to take, to grasp mentally (from Latin capere, via concipere 'to form an idea' -- the same root that appears as -ceive in perceive)

Suffix — -ed

Suffix — -ed: having, marked by (English)

Put it together

Put it together: Conceited comes from conceit: con- ('with, together,' intensifying) + ceit (from Latin capere, 'to take, grasp mentally,' via concipere 'to form an idea') + -ed ('marked by') -- the same Latin root that appears as -ceive in the everyday word perceive.

Use the root in a new word: perceive

Use the root in a new word: perceive: Even from the back row, she could perceive the smallest change in the conductor's expression.

Word Choice

Conceited almost always carries disapproval -- it describes pride that has become excessive and unpleasant to be around, not healthy self-respect.
